title: Reporting a School Energy Audit
text:
Students in an environmental science class completed a month-long energy audit of their school building. The project was not designed to produce a complete engineering study. Instead, the class wanted to identify simple patterns that could guide future questions about electricity use.

Teams recorded whether classroom lights and projectors were left on during lunch, after classes, and during several weekend activities. They also reviewed monthly electricity bills from the previous year. The students found that unnecessary lighting was common in a few hallways and shared rooms, but the billing records did not allow them to determine exactly how much electricity those lights used by themselves.

The class prepared a short report for the school administration. The report recommends clearer shutdown reminders and a two-month trial in which selected rooms are checked at the end of each day. Students suggest comparing those observations with the same period from the previous year, while also recording major schedule changes that might affect electricity use.

The teacher reminded students not to claim that the audit proved a particular cause of the school’s total energy use. Weather, air-conditioning demand, weekend events, and equipment changes can all influence the monthly bill. The report therefore separates what students directly observed from what they still need to test. Before publication, the class is editing the report for concise wording, clear pronoun references, correct capitalization, and punctuation that helps readers follow the limits of the evidence.

The students are also revising a table that lists their observations by location and time of day. The table will appear beside a short explanation of what the observations can and cannot show. For example, seeing lights on in an empty room confirms that electricity was being used at that moment, but it does not reveal the room's total share of the monthly bill. The class wants the wording around the table to preserve that distinction.

During peer review, students will underline every sentence that states a conclusion and circle the evidence used to support it. If a conclusion sounds more certain than the evidence allows, they will revise the wording before checking grammar and punctuation. The final editing pass will then focus on sentence boundaries, possessives, transitions, and unnecessary phrases so that language errors do not make the report's cautious reasoning harder to follow.
